title: A Winter for the Well
premise: Kestrel Quintana has spent his career hearing the dying count backwards—a private arithmetic of departure he's learned to ignore. When an excavation crew beneath the old Marrow Hill sanatorium unearths a door sealed from the inside, the counting spreads to the living, and Kestrel discovers his gift is actually a lineage: the Well below has always needed a keeper who hears it, and it has chosen him. To survive, he must learn the song's last verse without singing along, because the verse is a bargain—sing it whole and you keep your name but lose everyone you've counted; refuse, and the Well takes the town. In the end Kestrel sings only half the verse, trading his own voice and memory of every patient he's loved for the town's silence, becoming the new thing behind the sealed door—alive, listening, counting.
about_author: S. M. Nystrom is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent six years in palliative wards across the upper Midwest before turning to writing. Their fiction explores what the dying know and what the living agree not to hear.

chapters.title: The Arithmetic of Leaving
chapters.summary: Kestrel, POV: on his hospice rounds, patients count backwards under their breath—forty-one, forty—and he keeps their doors counted and lights on like rituals that hold something off. He tells no one. Emotional beat: weary tenderness masking dread; establish his competence and isolation.

chapters.title: What the Excavator Found
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: called to Marrow Hill's converted care facility when a construction crew unearths a stone door, sealed from the inside, its hinges worn smooth by use. A foreman has already begun counting backwards. Emotional beat: recognition—the door is familiar the way a face is.

chapters.title: Lights On, Doors Counted
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: back home, the counting follows him through the walls; his neighbor Mrs. Adeyemi pauses mid-sentence to murmur numbers. He reinforces his rituals, realizes they were taught to him by his grandmother, never explained. Emotional beat: the comfort of routine curdling into complicity.

chapters.title: The Sanatorium's Patient Ledger
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV with archival interludes: in the county records he finds the 1911 ledger—every death at Marrow Hill recorded as a number descending, and a nurse's marginalia: 'It counts them down so we don't have to.' Emotional beat: horror of inheritance; he was always meant to find this.

chapters.title: Half a Verse
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: an elderly former groundskeeper, Ivo Pell, hums a fragment of a lullaby and stops himself violently. 'There's a last verse,' he says. 'You learn it or you become it.' He refuses to teach it. Emotional beat: desperate hope meeting deliberate silence.

chapters.title: The First Living Number
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi POV: she reaches zero on her porch at dusk, smiling, and walks toward Marrow Hill through the snow. Kestrel follows and loses her at the excavation site, where the door is warm to the touch. Emotional beat: grief weaponized into urgency.

chapters.title: Chorus
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs: across town, the healthy begin counting—children in class, the barber mid-shave. The town council blames gas leaks; Kestrel knows better. Emotional beat: creeping communal denial, the horror of watching everyone rationalize.

chapters.title: Ivo's Confession
chapters.summary: Ivo POV: he was the last keeper's apprentice, sixty years ago; they sealed the door from inside because the keeper went in willingly to stop the singing, and the seal holds only while someone outside remembers the verse. He agrees to teach Kestrel—but the learning changes the learner. Emotional beat: guilt finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: Lessons in the Dark
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: Ivo teaches the first three verses in a root cellar lined with salt; each verse Kestrel masters quiets a district of the town. But the melody wants completing—it pulls his voice toward the ending. Emotional beat: empowerment shadowed by seduction.

chapters.title: The Door Is a Mouth
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: descending alone past the excavation, he touches the door and hears every counted soul still conscious behind it, including Mrs. Adeyemi, who begs him—not for rescue, but to hurry up and join them. Emotional beat: the dead aren't gone; they're conscripted.

chapters.title: What Survival Costs
chapters.summary: Ivo POV: flashback to 1963—Ivo sang the fourth verse to save his brother and forgot his brother entirely; the Well takes payment in memory. He warns Kestrel the last verse costs more than remembering. Emotional beat: love demonstrated through deliberate forgetting.

chapters.title: Zero Hour at St. Brigid's
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: the entire congregation reaches zero mid-service and rises together, walking in snow toward the hill. Kestrel sings the fourth verse publicly; hundreds stop, weeping, uncomprehending. The town now fears him. Emotional beat: savior recast as monster; power's first corruption.

chapters.title: The Committee of the Counted
chapters.summary: Councilwoman Reyes POV: she organizes the frightened town against Kestrel, then privately admits she can hear the numbers too and asks him to teach her. Emotional beat: fear breeding both mob and disciple; power attracts the corruptible.

chapters.title: Reyes Sings Ahead
chapters.summary: Reyes POV: impatient, she extracts verses from Ivo's old notebooks and sings the fifth alone; her district goes silent—but so does she, eyes open, counting nothing. The Well accepts partial payments eagerly. Emotional beat: ambition as an open door.

chapters.title: Ivo Reaches His Number
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: Ivo begins counting backwards after all these years—the Well calling in an old debt. Dying, he gives Kestrel the sixth verse and one rule: never sing the seventh alone, never sing it whole. Emotional beat: mentor's death as final lesson; grief without closure.

chapters.title: The Verse That Isn't Written
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: searching Ivo's effects, he finds the seventh verse exists nowhere on paper—it must be received at the door itself, which means going down. Behind him, the town's counting resumes, faster. Emotional beat: the trap closes; knowledge requires sacrifice.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: he enters the door at dawn, past corridors of the counted standing in rows, warm and waiting, Mrs. Adeyemi among them offering him his grandmother's voice. Emotional beat: temptation rendered as homecoming; identity dissolving at the threshold.

chapters.title: The Last Verse
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: at the Well's heart he receives the seventh verse whole—and understands it: sung completely, it frees the counted but erases the singer from every memory and record, unmade. Sung halfway, it seals the door again with the singer inside. Emotional beat: clarity at the point of no return.

chapters.title: Reyes at the Threshold
chapters.summary: Reyes POV, recovered but hollow: leading the town to the hill to drag Kestrel out, she finds the door open and hears him beginning the verse. She must choose: pull him back and doom the town, or let him finish. Emotional beat: redemption through restraint; witness as penance.

chapters.title: Halfway
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV: he sings to the middle of the seventh verse and stops—trading wholeness for the town. The door seals from the inside again, this time around him. Above, every counted soul wakes, remembering nothing but feeling kept. Emotional beat: sacrifice as authorship; he chooses the shape of his loss.

chapters.title: The Keeper Below
chapters.summary: Episodic POVs across the town: life resumes; a new hospice nurse is hired and finds the work strangely easy, the dying quiet. At Marrow Hill, visitors sometimes press a hand to the buried door and feel it listening. Emotional beat: peace purchased at an invisible price.

chapters.title: Counting Forward
chapters.summary: Kestrel POV, transformed: behind the door, he no longer counts backwards—he counts forward now, one, two, three, keeping time instead of taking it, holding the town's names in a memory that is slowly, mercifully forgetting his own. Final line: he begins to hum the first verse, gently, to no one. Emotional beat: bittersweet transcendence; survival redefined as service.
